## Question 1 (NHST Logic)

a) If my test has 70% power and an $\alpha$ of .01,{{< hp glyph="a" >}} what are my chances of making a Type I Error and a Type II Error?

b) If I wanted to reduce my chances of making each type of error,{{< hp glyph="a" >}} what could I change about my study/analysis?

## Question 2 (Statistical Hypotheses)

Download and use the [`penguins.csv`](../../data/penguins.csv){download="penguins.csv"} data file for this question. (Note that `body_mass` is given in grams, such that 4000 would mean 4 kilograms.)

a) My friend is arguing that penguins (across all three species) weigh, on average, 4000 grams. This doesn't sound right to me, so I want to approach this statistically.{{< hp glyph="a" >}} What should I use as my null hypothesis and what should I use as my alternative hypothesis?

b) Conduct a one-sample $t$-test of the null hypothesis from part (a). Report the $p$-value and your decision whether to retain or reject the null.

## Question 3 (p-values and Pragmatics)

Download and use the [`penguins.csv`](../../data/penguins.csv){download="penguins.csv"} data file for this question as well. This time, test the null hypothesis that penguins weigh, on average, 4150 grams.

a) Conduct a one-sample $t$-test of this null hypothesis. Report the observed test statistic and its degrees of freedom.

b) This test gives a much larger $p$-value than a test against 4000 grams would. Explain what the $p$-value in *this* test means and how it should be interpreted statistically.{{< hp glyph="a" >}} Your answer should go beyond merely stating whether it was significant, and should address why testing a different null value changes the $p$-value even though the data never changed.
